column3: Near-verbatim parallel: human willing is stated within Allah's willing; the added Lordship universalizes the frame.
Places endurance under the Lord's judgment and watchfulness, illuminating the wise governance named in 76:30.
Confessed dependence on taught knowledge parallels the closing Alim-Hakim, though it addresses knowing rather than willing.
Parallel nested-will formula for remembering; it keeps human response present while conditioning it on Allah's willing.
The immediately preceding invitation joins whoever wills to taking a way to the Lord, which 76:30 qualifies.
Attributes gift and knowledge to Allah, a limited resonance with dependence and divine knowledge.
Commands discerned obedience and non-obedience under Allah as Knowing, Wise; only indirectly relates to 76:30.
The nearby command to endure the Lord's judgment supplies the lived discipline surrounding the final will statement.
Contrasts human claims with Allah's knowledge of all in heavens and earth, reinforcing the asymmetry in 76:30.
Shared pain and distinct hope are linked to Allah's Knowing, Wise judgment, without an explicit will relation.
Following revelation and awaiting Allah's judgment presents human action within an outcome not self-controlled.
Allah's knowledge frames distinct bonds and priorities; its connection to the will clause is general.
Revelation occurs by Allah's permission and as He wills, adding a mode of divinely governed communication.
The Quran's deliberate sending grounds the reminder and way that precede 76:30.
The Quran is received from One described as Wise, Knowing, directly echoing 76:30's closing attributes.
A detailed ordinance closes with Knowing, Wise, showing those attributes in legal ordering rather than willing.
The question about wanting gods besides Allah concerns rival worship, not the nested willing of 76:30.
Creation from a thing can support creaturely dependence; a proposed will-link remains secondary and indirect.
Inheritance apportionment ends with Knowing, Wise, an analogous but distant instance of ordered judgment.
Reward for their striving provides the local outcome for the human response and endurance developed in the surah.
Gathering under the Wise, Knowing Lord extends those attributes to final collection and judgment.
An exception by Allah's willing and the superiority of divine knowledge constrain even successful human planning.
The challenge exposes deficient assumptions about the Lord of the worlds, relevant as a contrary posture to 76:30.
Whoever wills may remember, a close parallel for real human reception before a later divine-will qualification.
Remedy for unintended killing ends with Knowing, Wise, but does not clarify human will itself.
The same divine first-person willing governs replacement after human creation and strengthening, emphasizing contingency.
Limits interpretive willing by Allah's exclusive knowledge of ultimate interpretation and by stable verses.
Return is excepted by Allah's willing, while all-encompassing knowledge and trust accompany the contingency.
Reward for patience parallels the surah's moral sequence, though it does not state the will relation.
Release from oaths is attributed to Allah as Protector, Knowing, Wise, an example of measured divine ordering.
Allah's expansive provision and wisdom after separation offer a general image of non-humanly exhausted possibility.
Commanded remembrance is a nearby practice that links 76:29's reminder with 76:30's condition of willing.
Revelation is sent with Allah's knowledge and witnessed by Him, supporting the governed source of the reminder.
Personal acquisition of sin under Knowing, Wise judgment supports accountability without resolving will and agency.
Universal praise concludes a judgment sequence; it is a broad Lordship resonance only.
Lord of the worlds is present, but the proposed marker reading is secondary and does not add to 76:30.
Remembering recited signs and wisdom connects remembrance with a divinely communicated wise order.
Measured vessels echo order and measure in the surah, but add little to the will and knowledge claim.
Allah knows what is hidden and disclosed, concretizing the comprehensive knowledge in 76:30.
Gratitude and faith meet Allah as Appreciative, Knowing; this is only a general accountability parallel.
An appeal for judgment by truth and reliance on the Merciful illustrates deferring decisive judgment to Allah.
Created false objects cannot create anything; the suggested knowledge extension is too indirect for 76:30.
Seeking forgiveness invokes mercy and forgiveness, with no close link to nested willing or wisdom.
Refusing to seek reward or thanks gives a local example of intention not treated as self-serving possession.
The contrast between people and knowers is not a direct exposition of Allah's willing or the 76:30 closure.
Explicitly conditions future intention on Allah's willing and joins this with remembrance and guidance.
A choice over who acts first has no substantive connection to the divine-human will relation.
Offers a contrary misuse of divine willing: occurrence is wrongly turned into a warrant for worship without knowledge.
Amazement at one God is a weak thematic contrast to exclusive divine willing and knowledge.
The next verse specifies Allah's willing as admission into mercy while holding the wrongdoers' outcome alongside it.
Allah places tranquility and increases faith, ending with Knowing, Wise; it shows divinely enabled inner response.
Guidance is preceded by clarification of what to guard against, relating knowledge to ordered responsibility.
A contrary scene: patience or impatience is equal once recompense is due, distinguishing final inevitability from present choice.
Allah wills to clarify, guide, and turn toward people, linking divine will to intelligible guidance and restoration.
Repentance and return occur under Allah's Knowing, Wise description, but without an explicit will formula.
Reward for patience is a close internal outcome for the disciplined response surrounding 76:30.
Lord of the worlds appears in a historical rebuke; its secondary marker association adds no clear value here.
Human intention to reconcile is met by Allah's bringing together, illustrating dependent completion rather than isolated agency.
The speaker disclaims possession of harm or right guidance, sharply limiting independent human control.
They defer disputed duration to the Lord's greater knowledge, then act carefully within their limited knowledge.
When Allah decrees a matter it comes to be, supplying a creation-and-decree context for encompassing will.
The named spring belongs to the surah's reward imagery but does not clarify 76:30's will claim.
Forbids closing tomorrow's act as certain; the next verse explicitly reopens it to Allah's willing.
Allah turns toward whom He wills and is Knowing, Wise, linking will with non-arbitrary restoration after conflict.
Blessing the Lord's majestic, generous name is a remote doxological parallel only.
Layered punishment and ignorance relate broadly to divine judgment, while the alternate reading is not needed for 76:30.
Affliction is by Allah's permission, while belief brings guidance to the heart; it portrays dependent response under knowledge.
The surah has already shown the way and named grateful or ungrateful response, framing the choice in 76:29-30.
Universal dominion and witness over every thing reinforce Allah's encompassing oversight; an active-will inference remains secondary.
Wise divine recompense is explicit, but the verse contributes little about human willing.
Restricted touching by the purified concerns access and purity, not the will and knowledge relation.
Deferred knowing after heedless hope provides a distant temporal contrast to Allah's present knowledge.
All things are within the Lord's knowledge, and feared events remain excepted by His willing; this closely joins both themes.
Exclusive calling on the Lord and rejection of association provide a doctrinal boundary for speaking of Allah's will.
Unreduced produce supplies a narrative contrast between received abundance and mistaken self-assurance.
Allah knows what is invoked besides Him and is Mighty, Wise, connecting false reliance to comprehensive divine judgment.
Inherited practice is reported without an explicit account of divine will, knowledge, or the way in 76:30.
Praise across this world and the next rests on Allah as Wise, Aware, a broad eschatological echo of 76:30.
The messenger brings truth from the Lord amid Allah's ownership, knowledge, and wisdom, situating response under divine sufficiency.
The question about objects of worship is preparatory polemic, with no direct addition to nested willing.
Allah's knowledge of secret and public speech limits the authority of hostile claims and supports the Alim clause.
Even overwhelming signs do not yield faith except by Allah's willing; it is a difficult parallel preserving human ignorance.
Ancient ancestors are named as objects of inherited worship, without a direct will or knowledge contribution.
Peace upon Noah among the worlds is a blessing formula; its secondary marker reading remains too remote.
Messengers cannot bring authority except by Allah's permission, while favor reaches whom He wills; agency is explicitly bounded.
Equating others with the Lord of the worlds is contrary worship language but does not develop 76:30's terms.
Allah creates and oversees every thing, furnishing a comprehensive dependence frame while leaving human willing unelaborated.
No soul believes except by Allah's permission, a close parallel for enabled rather than self-originating human response.
The Quran's descent from the Lord of the worlds reinforces the divine source of the reminder, without stating the will relation.
Future knowing warns that present dispute will be answered; it only broadly echoes the knowledge horizon of 76:30.
Opposition to Allah and His messenger ends in punishment, but contains no direct contribution on willing or wisdom.
Human willing is expressed as advancing or delaying; with 74:56 it forms a close parallel preserving choice under divine willing.
Allah brings about a settled matter so that destruction and life occur on clear evidence, linking decree with accountable disclosure.
Commands to speak about Allah without knowledge show a contrary epistemic posture to the Alim-Hakim conclusion.
A prophet disclaims power over another before Allah and turns in trust, illustrating non-possession of ultimate outcomes.
Every thing has stores with Allah and descends only by known measure, portraying controlled divine disposition.
The wind runs by Solomon's command; delegated command is a distant example of power received rather than autonomous.
A call to follow another path cannot transfer the follower's sins, preserving personal responsibility within dependence.
Directs doubt toward prior readers and received truth, a limited parallel for the externally given reminder.
Questions any claim to see the unseen, contrasting human epistemic pretension with the knowledge asserted in 76:30.
Allah guides whom He wills amid human disagreement, connecting guidance to divine choosing and disclosed judgment.
The declaration that Allah does what He wills supplies a general sovereignty parallel, without the human-will wording.
Transfer of dominion, honor, and abasement occurs by divine willing, widening the scope of contingent outcomes.
Allah's bounty is given to whom He wills and He is all-encompassing, Knowing, joining will, gift, and knowledge.
Forgiveness and punishment are assigned to whom Allah wills under His ownership of all, a close outcome parallel.
No soul dies except by Allah's permission and a fixed writing; this is adjacent to dependence but concerns death.
Allah chooses whom He wills from messengers for disclosure of the unseen, limiting human access to hidden knowledge.
Allah forgives whom He wills while associating others is excluded, directly linking divine willing to judgment.
Allah purifies whom He wills and no one is wronged, showing divine selection alongside non-arbitrary justice.
Allah's favor, teaching, and protection surround the messenger, portraying knowledge and wisdom as enabling rather than self-owned.
Allah can remove people and bring others if He wills, closely paralleling 76:28's replacement motif.
Allah creates what He wills and owns heaven and earth, grounding created existence in unrestricted divine agency.
Allah forgives and punishes whom He wills within universal ownership, a direct judgment parallel.
Allah punishes and forgives whom He wills; divine power frames the alternatives of final outcome.
Allah could have made one community but tests distinct communities; this complicates uniformity claims about divine willing.
Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, explicitly pairing guidance with divine choice.
Had Allah willed, association would not occur; this states contingency while not treating occurrence as approval.
Had the Lord willed, hostile plotting would not occur; it frames opposition within divine permission without endorsing it.
Whomever Allah wills to guide is opened to submission, while misguidance is portrayed as constriction.
The self-sufficient, merciful Lord can replace people if He wills, closely supporting 76:28-30's creaturely contingency.
Allah could have guided all people had He willed, a direct counterfactual about collective guidance.
Allah could afflict later peoples for their sins and seal hearts; it adds a judgmental possibility to divine willing.
Moses says Allah misguides and guides whom He wills, while seeking mercy and forgiveness; a direct but difficult parallel.
Allah's mercy reaches whom He wills, joining divine willing with a moral order of reverence and giving.
Human action is denied independent efficacy in a decisive event, supporting dependence while retaining enacted participation.
Allah comes between a person and the heart, a close limitation on self-possession and independent interior control.
Reverence brings a criterion and forgiveness, connecting response to divinely granted discernment.
Allah does not change a favor until people change what is within themselves, preserving meaningful human response.
Allah enriches whom He wills from His bounty and is Knowing, Wise, linking provision to those attributes.
Had the Lord willed, all on earth would believe; this is a central parallel for collective faith and divine will.
If Allah intends harm none can remove it, and His favor reaches whom He wills; outcomes are not independently mastered.
Advice cannot benefit when Allah wills to leave a people astray, a contrary and severe nested-agency formulation.
Enduring punishment is excepted by what the Lord wills, preserving a qualification at the horizon of final judgment.
Enduring felicity is likewise excepted by what the Lord wills, pairing the preceding qualification across outcomes.
Allah prevails in His affair while people often do not know, linking governing purpose and limited human knowledge.
Allah grants mercy to whom He wills and does not waste the reward of doers, holding gift and action together.
The Lord is subtle in what He wills and is Knowing, Wise, closely echoing 76:30's attributes.
Allah does not change a people's condition until they change themselves, an important counterbalance for human response.
Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns, pairing divine will with turning response.
Had Allah willed He could have guided all people, another direct counterfactual for universal guidance.
Allah effaces and confirms what He wills while the source book remains with Him, linking will to ordered inscription.
Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, ending with Mighty, Wise rather than arbitrary power.
Allah can remove people and bring a new creation if He wills, a broader replacement parallel to 76:28.
Had Allah willed He could have guided all; the verse also distinguishes a straight way from a deviating one.
Allah could make one community, yet guides and leaves astray whom He wills while holding people answerable.
Whoever wills the immediate is granted from it to whom Allah wills, then faces consequence; human and divine willing are layered.
The Lord knows people best and may show mercy or punish if He wills, linking knowledge to outcome.
Allah could take away revealed communication if He willed, showing the reminder itself as contingent gift.
Whomever Allah guides is guided, and whomever He leaves astray lacks a guiding protector; guidance is not self-secured.
Whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve, a major human-choice parallel that must remain alongside 76:30.
A divinely decided matter and a sign for people frame the birth narrative as enacted decree.
The Creator gives each thing its form and then guides it, connecting creation with directed capacity.
Allah admits believers who do good into gardens; Allah does what He intends, joining response with divine effective will.
Allah guides whom He intends through clear signs, another revelation-and-guidance parallel.
Allah does whatever He wills amid universal prostration and differentiated humiliation, stressing sovereign action.
Allah admits believers into gardens and does what He intends, an outcome parallel to 76:31.
The objection that Allah could have sent angels if He willed illustrates a contrary inference from divine capacity.
Allah purifies whom He wills after warning against following steps of evil, coupling command, response, and divine purification.
Allah guides to His light whom He wills; this supplies a major illumination-and-guidance form of divine enabling.
Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path after sending clear signs, directly linking disclosure and divine choice.
Allah can make better things if He wills; it presents unrealized possibility as subject to divine decision.
Whoever wills may take a way to the Lord, a near parallel to 76:29 that belongs beside its qualification.
The messenger does not guide whom he loves; Allah guides whom He wills and knows the guided, a central parallel.
The Lord creates and chooses what He wills, while choice is denied independent standing; it directly bears on agency language.
Allah punishes whom He wills and shows mercy to whom He wills, then all return to Him.
Allah gives victory to whom He wills and is Mighty, Merciful, treating historical outcome as divinely bestowed.
Had Allah willed He could have given every soul its guidance, yet the stated outcome unfolds otherwise.
No one can shield people when Allah intends harm or mercy, sharply denying independent control of outcomes.
Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, warning against grief over those choices.
A contrary fatalistic argument uses Allah's possible will to refuse feeding; it is essential beside 43:20 as misuse of the premise.
Allah created people and what they do, a foundational but interpretively weighty dependence claim.
Allah guides with the Book whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills, tying guidance to revelation and response.
Whomever Allah guides cannot be misled, directly depicting the effective side of divine guidance.
Allah sends the spirit by His command upon whom He wills, linking revelation to sovereign selection.
The Allah-purpose formula excludes injustice toward servants, qualifying divine determination with justice.
Allah decides what He wills after messengers' signs; decisive judgment remains with Him.
Allah could make people one community, but admits whom He wills into mercy; a central plurality-and-mercy parallel.
Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns, holding selection and turning together.
Allah gives daughters or sons to whom He wills and makes whom He wills barren; creaturely conditions are distributed by will.
A person follows desire with knowledge and is left astray by Allah, a difficult contrary case for self-directed willing.
The messenger disclaims knowledge of what will be done to himself or others, resisting human claims over future outcome.
None can control Allah's intended harm or benefit; this closely states the non-possession implied by 76:30.
Allah forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills under universal dominion, a direct final-outcome parallel.
Intercession has no effect except after Allah permits whom He wills and approves, distinguishing permission from independent action.
All things are created by measure, supplying a concise order-and-determination context for 76:30's wisdom.
Allah determines death and is not outstripped, limiting human control over life and final succession.
Allah can replace people with their likenesses and produce them in an unknown form, a close parallel to 76:28.
Allah gives His bounty to whom He wills; divine gift is stated as unrestricted grace.
Allah gives mercy to whom He wills and holds bounty in His hand, linking access to grace with divine choice.
Allah has written that He and His messengers will prevail, an inscription-of-outcome parallel.
Allah gives His bounty to whom He wills and is possessor of great bounty, reinforcing non-owned grace.
Allah's command reaches its measure and He has set a measure for every thing, directly supporting wise ordering.
A reminder is followed by whoever wills taking a way to the Lord, the closest omitted companion to 76:29.
The reminder is available to whoever wills to remember, immediately before 74:56's divine-will qualification.
Whoever among people wills to be upright is the human-will half of the 81:29 parallel already present.
Allah knows the declared and what is hidden, a compact parallel for the Alim clause.
Two ways are shown, providing a concise human-path framework for 76:3 and 76:29-30.
Guidance is stated as resting upon Allah, a compact source-and-responsibility parallel.
